Q: How should a React app handle API data when the user navigates away before the request finishes? A:

Should I...

  • Cancel the request using AbortController
  • Simply ignore the response after unmounting
  • Keep the response in a cache for when the user returns
  • Use a data-fetching library such as React Query

Basically, yes, attempt to do all of these when possible and where it makes sense.

Cancel the request using AbortController

You should attempt to cancel any in-flight requests. You possibly conserve client-side resources by cancelling early, and some backend/service/APIs are capable of receiving the cancellation request and can quit early server-side to also conserve resources.

Simply ignore the response after unmounting

You can ignore any response that arrives after cancellation or after the component has otherwise already unmounted. FYI any enqueued state updates after unmounting are now a non-op and ignored by React anyway.

Keep the response in a cache for when the user returns / Use a data-fetching library such as React Query

Caching responses is a very sensible thing to do, and data-fetching libraries like Redux-Toolkit Query, React-Query, etc., generally handle this out-of-the-box for you. This is beneficial when a user maybe navigates back to the first page where you can simply serve the cached data and save a network call for stuff that was literally just fetched. Again, this is a way to help conserve resources.

Q: "no 'operator++(int)' declared for postfix '++' [-fpermissive]" on enums A:

No, you are wrong, there is no such operator.

To get the next one, convert your value to an int (or std::underlying_type_t<E>), increment it, then static_cast it back to your enum. Note that going out of bounds can eventually lead to undefined behaviour, so checks are a good idea.

Q: What are the important notions in C that you did not learn from your teachers? A:

It would be beneficial if the students were at some point exposed to tools that can help them write cleaner, better code. The tools may not all be relevant to them at this stage, but knowing what is available helps.

  • Debuggers - GDB, TotalView, etc.
  • Static/dynamic analysers - splint, Valgrind, ...
  • Unit testing frameworks - CUnit, cmockery, Check, ...
  • Documentation management - Doxygen, ...
  • Build management - Make, memoize, fabricate, ...
  • Code metrics - CCCC, Understand, SLOCCount, ...
  • Code coverage - Gcov, LCOV, etc.

One should also stress the use of different (!) compilers with strict compiler warning flags and attending to each and every warning message.

Q: Updating one of Python's previous versions to its latest version for bug fixes A:

You can pass a specific version to py install. If only you pass a major version and --update, it will update it to the most recent minor version.

For example, if you have 3.12.2 installed,

py install --update 3.12

Will update it to 3.12.10.

Q: if (n!=0) n=0; v/s n=0; Which is more efficient and why? A:

If n is a 2's complement integral type or an unsigned integral type, then writing n = 0 directly will certainly be no slower than the version with the condition check, and a good optimising compiler will generate the same code. Some compilers compile assignment to zero as XOR'ing a register value with itself, which is a single instruction.

If n is a floating point type, a 1s' complement integral type, or a signed magnitude integral type, then the two code snippets differ in behaviour. E.g. if n is signed negative zero for example. (Acknowledge @chqrlie.) Also if n is a pointer on a system than has multiple null pointers representations, then if (n != 0) n = 0; will not assign n, when n is one of the various null pointers. n = 0; imparts a different functionality.

"will always be more efficient" is not true. Should reading n have a low cost, writing n a high cost (Think of re-writing non-volatile memory that needs to re-write a page) and is likely n == 0, then n = 0; is slower, less efficient than if (n != 0) n = 0;.
